newsitem.title: USA: Power co-ops fear TVA rate hikes and bigger debt.
newsitem.headline: Power co-ops fear TVA rate hikes and bigger debt.

text.p: Rural and municipal power distributors Wednesday raised concern that the Tennessee Valley Authority was trying to stifle market competition in moves that could come back to haunt taxpayers and ratepayers.

Customers of TVA, the nation's largest public power supplier, accused the agency of using "scare tactics" to discourage distributors of its electricity, mainly rural and municipal utilities, from buying power from other suppliers.

"TVA, a non-profit federal agency, has done everything it could to frustrate our efforts to take advantage of free competition in the marketplace," David Fletcher, chairman of Bristol Virginia Utilities Board, said at a House energy and power subcommittee hearing on deregulation and public power.
The massive agency is saddled with about $28 billion in debt. Although its bonds are not backed by the Treasury, lawmakers said if TVA defaulted, the burden might ultimately fall on taxpayers.

TVA and distributors said as Congress moved to deregulate electricity markets, it should allow TVA to sell power to customers outside its traditional territory, a move that neighboring investor-owned utilities are trying to block.

"If (TVA) does not have this flexibility, then its only choice is to raise its rates to its remaining distributors to cover its operating costs and debt service," said James Baker, speaking for the Tennessee Valley Public Power Association.

Bristol, which buys 600 million kilowatt hours of power annually from TVA, challenged the agency by signing a seven-year contract from next year with Cinergy Corp through which it would save a total of $70 million.
In retaliation, TVA tried to intimidate other distributors, saying the new power supplies would be less reliable than TVA's, Fletcher said.
He added that TVA was trying to steal Bristol's industrial customers by offering them electricity at 2 percent below any rate Bristol might offer.

"TVA could never expect to recover the cost of new facilities necessary to directly serve our customers with such predatory prices," he said. "This kind of fiscal irresponsibility can only increase TVA's already huge $27 billion debt."

TVA chief operating officer Joe Dickey said the agency was able to offer the low rates to industrial customers and not to Bristol just as other power suppliers offered widely varying rates to industrial, residential and commercial customers.
He said the agency was not trying to scare customers into staying with TVA power, but wanted to make clear that "TVA has proven to be a reliable source of power in the past."

TVA is seeking $54 million from Bristol to cover losses on facilities it built to serve the utility, although TVA had seven years notice that the distributor was not going to renew its contract and the agency expected to be able easily to replace the Bristol's demand, Fletcher said.

Dickey said no specific units had been dedicated to serving Bristol, but the agency based its $54 million claim on lost revenue as defined by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. Bristol is contesting the claim at the commission.
